newsitem.title: USA: U.S jobs report fails to clarify rate hike picture.
newsitem.headline: U.S jobs report fails to clarify rate hike picture.

text.p: The U.S. employment picture remained healthy in February but the data released by the Labor Department on Friday did not seem likely, by themselves, to push the Federal Reserve closer to an official interest rate hike, economists said.

The government reported that non-farm payrolls grew by 339,000 jobs in February, exceeding the 230,000 average estimate economists had offered in a Reuters poll. But January and December payrolls growth were both revised downward, January's by 24,000 jobs and December's by 30,000 jobs.
Bond prices momentarily dropped when traders read the headline on payroll growth, but prices recovered when the rest of the data mitigated the impact of the initial headline.

Investors had feared that the unemployment rate might drop to 5.2 percent in February from 5.4 percent in January, a fall that would have been read as a sign of a very tight labor market. Instead, the unemployment rate returned to its 5.3 percent prevailing trend, offering bond investors some relief.
Fearful of wage pressures that would eventually lead to price inflation, bond investors had expected average hourly wages to rise by four cents. Instead, they rose by three.
Factory jobs, which traditionally pay higher wages, declined by 2,000.
A big part of the payrolls growth occurred in construction, where payrolls grew by 109,000 jobs, a surge the Labor Department attributed to unseasonably mild weather.

"This report does not change things dramatically in terms of Federal Reserve policy," said David Sloan, senior economist at consulting firm I.D.E.A. Inc. "The payroll growth number was above expectations at 339,000. The main strength was in construction, which the Labor Department tied to mild weather. The hourly earnings data didn't cause much of a scare."

While economists said the February employment report by itself might not decisively push the Federal Reserve toward a tightening move, John Williams, managing director and chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust, argued that clear justification for a Fed tightening has been established.

"Given the Fed's recent foot dragging, I suspect they will not tighten on March 25 (at the Federal Open Market Committee meeting), but I think the odds of a tightening on May 20 are extremely high," said Williams.
Average job growth of 272,000 a month over the last three months "far exceeds" the sustainable pace of 150,000, he said.
Williams said an average workweek length of 35 hours demonstrates a lot of economic activity.
"When you have a lot of people working a lot of hours, they must be making a lot of stuff," he said.
That activity could translate into Gross Domestic Product growth of 2.5 percent to 3.0 percent in the first quarter, said Williams, "well above the non-inflationary speedlimit for the ecomony."
"With the labor market simmering, the emergence of wage and cost pressures is imminent," he said.
